content_html:
Every year, at the top of the hills surrounding Cusco, one of the most emblematic and least known festivities of the Andean calendar is celebrated: the Velacuy Cross. This deeply symbolic ceremony is a bridge between the ancestral worldview of the Andes and the Christian traditions brought by the Spanish colonizers.

What is the Velacuy Cross?

“Velacuy” comes from Quechua and means “to watch” or “to keep vigil.” So, Cruz Velacuy it is literally the evening of the cross. It is celebrated every year on May 3, coinciding with the Day of the Holy Cross in the Catholic calendar. However, in Cusco and other Andean regions, this date takes on a unique meaning: it is the time of reconnect with the earth, the apus (mountain spirits) and the ancestors.

Rites at dawn

The night before, families or communities climb to the peaks where there are protective crosses, located on hills or sacred places. There is a vigil filled with offerings, candles, traditional music and dances. The cross is asked for protection, favorable rains, health and good harvests.

The Andean and the Christian are intertwined: the crosses are decorated with flowers, coca leaves, multicolored flags (wiphala) and sometimes even Catholic elements such as rosaries or images of saints. At dawn, with the first rays of the sun, the community celebrates with bonfires, potlucks and dancing.

An act of cultural syncretism

Cruz Velacuy is not only a religious ceremony, it is also a reaffirmation of identity and cultural resistance. Since colonial times, the Andean peoples adapted the cult of the cross to their own spiritual landscape, generating a syncretism that still beats on every hill in Cusco.

Where to live it?

The hills like Pachatusan, Sacsayhuamán, Cerro Picol and other sacred points around Cusco are classic settings for this ceremony. If you are in Cusco in May, it is a unique opportunity to experience the living spirituality of the Andes.
